name: 'Might makes right' doctrines (Thrasymachus and Callicles)
plain_explanation: Two figures in Plato's dialogues argue that justice is really nothing but whatever benefits the powerful, and that laws restraining the strong are just a convenient trick invented by the weak.
precise_definition: Thrasymachus's position (Republic, Book I) that there is no justice except the interest of the stronger and that laws are made by governments for their own advantage, with no impersonal standard for appeal; and Callicles's similar position (Gorgias) that the law of nature is the law of the stronger, with conventional institutions and moral precepts invented by the weak to restrain the strong.
why_it_mattered: Russell explicitly notes these doctrines have won wider assent in the twentieth century (his own day) than in antiquity, and stresses that, whatever their merit, they are 'not characteristic of the Sophists' as a whole, correcting a common conflation.
historical_origin: Attributed by Plato to Thrasymachus and Callicles as dramatic interlocutors.
competing_positions: Protagoras's practical defense of law and convention as socially necessary, which is not a might-makes-right position
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes, writing in the 1940s, that such doctrines 'have won much wider assent in our day than they did in antiquity,' a clear contemporary allusion.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly concerns the foundations of political legitimacy and law.
